fr:title.text: Can multi-step bootstrapping match Dyna with a perfect model?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Can multi-step bootstrapping match Dyna with a perfect model?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The nonplanning method in the maze example is a special case of the n-step method. Could a multi-step bootstrapping method do as well as a Dyna agent given a perfect model?

html:details.html:p: Take n large enough and the first pass is just as good, in the sense that every (s,a) pair on the encountered trajectory gets updated. But Dyna updates from Q-values that have themselves been updated, so it is not confined to the n-step trajectory it actually walked. That extra reach is what an n-step method cannot reproduce, so I do not think it can match Dyna even with a perfect model.

fr:title.text: When skewed transition probabilities favor sample updates

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: When skewed transition probabilities favor sample updates

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Suppose the branching factor b is large but the transition probabilities are highly skewed, so a few successors are far more likely than the rest. Does this strengthen or weaken the case for sample updates over expected updates?

html:details.html:p: It strengthens it. Samples concentrate where the probability mass is, so a handful of them recovers most of what the expected update computes — and the expected update pays for the whole tail to get there.

fr:title.text: The spikes in the optimistic-initialization curve

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The spikes in the optimistic-initialization curve

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Optimistic initialization produces oscillations and a pronounced early spike in the optimal-action curve. Why?

html:details.html:p: Every arm on the testbed has support well below 5, so an unpulled arm's optimistic estimate beats the empirical estimate of anything already pulled. The early steps are therefore a round robin over all arms, and — with rewards deterministic — the optimal arm keeps being pulled until its estimate falls below the remaining optimistic ones. That alternation between "sweep the untried" and "exploit the best so far" is the oscillation.

fr:title.text: The UCB spike at step 11

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The UCB spike at step 11

fr:mainmatter.html:p: UCB performance shows a pronounced spike on the 11th step of the 10-armed testbed, then drops. Why?

html:details.html:p: With 10 arms at equal initialization the exploration bonus forces the first 10 pulls to be a round robin. On step 11 all bonuses are equal again, so the tie is broken by empirical reward and the best-so-far arm is pulled — the spike. It drops immediately after, because that pull shrinks the chosen arm's bonus and hands the next steps to other, possibly worse, arms.

fr:title.text: Where to draw the agent-environment boundary

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Where to draw the agent-environment boundary

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Where should the line between agent and environment be drawn — at the steering wheel, at the muscles, at the intent to drive somewhere? Is any level fundamentally preferable?

html:details.html:p: Draw it where you can already execute the behavior that carries you from one state to another. Fixing the boundary above the level of reliable control means the agent must relearn what it already has; fixing it below means solving a control problem you did not need to solve. This is precisely the premise of hierarchical reinforcement learning, which raises the boundary over time by learning subpolicies and then treating them as primitive.

fr:title.text: The maze-runner that never learns to hurry

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The maze-runner that never learns to hurry

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A maze-running agent gets +1 for escaping and 0 otherwise, and after many episodes shows no improvement. What is going wrong?

html:details.html:p: The task has not actually been communicated. Every escaping trajectory earns the same return regardless of how long it took, so the agent has no reason to prefer a fast escape to a slow one. Fix it by paying -1 per timestep, or by discounting so that a reward collected later is worth less.

fr:title.text: Return of an infinite constant reward stream

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Return of an infinite constant reward stream

fr:mainmatter.html:p: With \gamma = 0.9, a reward of 2 followed by an infinite sequence of 7s, what are G_1 and G_0?

html:details.html:p: Peel off the leading term and sum the geometric tail:
html:details.fr:tex: \begin {align*} G_0 &= R_{1} + \gamma R_{2} + \gamma ^2 R_{3} + \cdots \\ &= 2 + \sum _{i = 1}^{\infty } \gamma ^{i} R_{i} \\ &= 2 + \gamma \sum _{i = 0}^{\infty } \gamma ^{i} R_{i + 2} \\ &= 2 + \frac {7 \gamma }{1 - \gamma } \\ &= 65 \end {align*}
html:details.html:p: and
html:details.fr:tex: \begin {align*} G_1 &= R_{2} + \gamma R_{2} + \gamma ^2 R_{3} + \cdots \\ &= 7 + \sum _{i = 1}^{\infty } \gamma ^{i} R_{i} \\ &= 7 + \gamma \sum _{i = 0}^{\infty } \gamma ^{i} R_{i + 3} \\ &= 7 + \frac {7 \gamma }{1 - \gamma } \\ &= 70 \end {align*}

fr:title.text: Why the same shift is not harmless in the episodic case

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the same shift is not harmless in the episodic case

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Does the previous exercise's conclusion survive in an episodic task? Give an example.

html:details.html:p: It does not. The shift is c summed over the episode's length, so it is not constant across states — v_c is larger for states from which episodes run longer. In the maze runner, a positive c therefore rewards dawdling, which is the exact opposite of the intended task.

fr:title.text: Tabular methods as linear function approximation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Tabular methods as linear function approximation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Show that tabular methods are a special case of linear function approximation. What are the feature vectors?

html:details.html:p: Linear function approximation carries two objects, \boldsymbol {w} and \boldsymbol {x}(s), updated as
html:details.fr:tex: w_{t + 1} = w_{t} + \alpha (r_t + \gamma w_{t}^{\top } x_{t+1} - w_t^{\top } x_t) x_t
html:details.html:p: The tabular setting is the one where we can afford a coordinate per state, x(s) \in \mathbb {R}^{|S|}. Take the features to be one-hot, x : s_i \mapsto \boldsymbol {e}_i, and identify
Substituting,
html:details.fr:tex: w_{t + 1} = w_{t} + \alpha (\mathbb {E}_{a \sim \pi , s \sim p}[r(s_i)] + v(s_{t + 1}) - v(s_{t})) \cdot \boldsymbol {e}_i
html:details.html:p: Since \boldsymbol {w} is the table of values and \boldsymbol {e}_i zeroes out everything else, updating the ith entry is exactly one tabular update to v_{\pi }(s_i). Generalization across states is precisely what the one-hot encoding refuses to do.

fr:title.text: Counting polynomial features

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Counting polynomial features

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why does (9.17) define (n + 1)^k distinct features for dimension k?

html:details.html:p: Each of the k state components s_j carries an exponent c_{i,j} chosen from \{0, 1, \ldots , n\} — that is n + 1 options — and the choices are independent, so there are (n + 1)^k distinct exponent vectors, hence that many features.

fr:title.text: Tile shape as a statement about generalization

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Tile shape as a statement about generalization

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Suppose you believe one of two state dimensions is more likely to have an effect on the value function than the other. What tilings could take advantage of that?

html:details.html:p: Use anisotropic tiles — long in the direction you want to generalize along, thin in the direction you do not. Reading the two state dimensions as (x, y) coordinates: to make states sharing an x coordinate resemble one another, tile with tall narrow rectangles. States at the same x then fall in a common vertical tile and share their features, while any change in x moves you into disjoint tiles. Tile shape is how a prior about which dimension matters gets stated.
